title: ThousandWorlds: A benchmark for emulating the climates of potentially habitable exoplanets
claim: A dataset is defined by its simulation count, a small set of input parameters, and a stack of multi-field gridded outputs.
layout: 3 boxed panels, left-to-right: dataset, inputs, outputs; icons and stacked maps
description: Three side-by-side rounded boxes read left to right. The left box, headed 'DATASET: N = 1689', shows three stacked rendered exoplanet globes: icy blue, Earth-like teal and white, and dark with a red hot spot. The middle box, 'INPUTS: (x, s) ∈ R^8 × {1,...,5}', lists eight black icons with labels: radius, surface gravity, rotation period, surface pressure, CO2 concentration, CH4 concentration, stellar flux and stellar temperature. A ninth entry, GCM label, covers the simulator index. The right box, 'OUTPUTS: y ∈ R^{32×64×53}', shows five stacks of lat-lon maps labeled temperature, humidity, clouds, winds and radiation. The maps use different colormaps: red/blue, purple/white, blue, streamlines, and plasma. The eye goes first to the colorful planet renders and the output maps.
caption: Dataset overview. Output fields are defined on a 32 × 64 latitude–longitude grid. There are 53 fields in total and ∼105 output dimensions.
abstract: The search for life beyond Earth will depend on detecting faint signatures in the atmospheres of potentially habitable exoplanets. Interpreting those signatures requires understanding the host planet's climate: the same molecule may signal life on one planet and abiotic chemistry on another. Global climate models (GCMs) provide this understanding, but individual runs can require up to millions of core-hours and substantial domain expert time. Machine-learning emulators could remove this bottleneck, but progress has been limited by the absence of a curated, multi-model exoclimate dataset. We introduce ThousandWorlds, an ML-ready benchmark for exoclimate emulation and for the broader regime of low-data, multi-simulator, parameter-to-field regression. The dataset contains approximately 1,700 simulations from five GCMs, mapping eight planet parameters to 3D atmospheric fields including temperature, humidity, winds, clouds, and radiation. Three nested subsets define progressively harder challenges: single-simulator regression, multi-simulator regression with complete observations, and multi-simulator regression with structured missingness. We propose two evaluation protocols: one for ranking methods, and one that measures performance relative to the disagreement between GCMs themselves. We evaluate ten baselines spanning simple methods, trees, deep learning, and Gaussian processes. GP-based methods perform best, suggesting that ThousandWorlds exposes a regime where off-the-shelf deep learning does not yet succeed. Data: https://doi.org/10.57967/hf/8695. Code: https://github.com/astroautomata/ThousandWorlds.
